rv.q: Staff Meal feels like a portal: We tumble through its funny, eerie evocation of the moment that made—is still making—our present, and we come out the other side feeling, for all its ebb toward emptiness, full.
The play's narrative components — a meet-cute, a culinary cult of personality — are familiar parts soldered together with an inventiveness that doesn't hold.
Director Morgan Green creates magic from scene to scene, whether they are linear or not, dream logic or that of frightening nightmares.
For those with an open mind and heart to new WTF experiences, you might find something delectable in this play.

Staff Meal has plenty of problems, including a lack of cohesion and a second half that is too vague to support its dark intentions, but it's always interesting when an artist adds fresh colors to his palette.
There’s enough great material in Staff Meal to furnish a half-dozen plays.
But everyone’s efforts can’t make up for the show’s directionlessness.
Staff Meal promises a nine-course tasting menu of strange theatrical flavors, but it turns out to be mostly kale.

Asking several audience members, I also got a mixed bag of understanding. Though interesting in all their perspectives, none of those points of view completely lined up with my take on it all either (covid, past lives, isolation, loneliness, restaurants, end of times, acts of service, shifting identities).

All too soon after Berry's interruption, we are heading back to the restaurant, to the dungeonlike wine cellar, and to painfully drawn-out sketches that play like college assignments for a class in Theater of the Absurd.
Like life, it's not perfect, with its ups and downs, but it provides fine fare that may not go down easy but feeds the soul in these harried times.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this surreal meta-comedy about modern dating and culinary culture. While some praise its unpredictability and absurdist risks, others find it undercooked despite its quirky ambitions.
